1. **The book now constructs the contour from proved estimates.**  
   Under RH, allowing multiple zeros, it controls the complete heat evolution at a fixed positive distance from the real axis for backward times of order \(1/(\log Y)^2\). Crucially, the error is relative to the potentially tiny xi field, including the entire Gaussian tail. This earns nonvanishing, then yields actual contours preserving \(H\,dz\), with controlled displacement, tangent, containment and height coverage. Earlier conservation identities alone did not establish those properties. [Book, Theorems 1.1 and 3.1](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:85)

2. **The contour has a precise, limited role in the multiplicity argument.**  
   Its zero-free corridor eliminates contributions through the upper and lower window transitions. The remaining “resource” is
   \[
   \mathcal R_Y
   =\text{earlier interior nonreal population}
   +\text{one-sided inward flux through the height ends}.
   \]
   The exact collision balance gives \(M_Y\le \tfrac32\mathcal R_Y\), where \(M_Y\) counts labels at nonsimple endpoint zeros. This is a sharp conversion from an estimate to a simplicity conclusion—but neither remaining term has a useful upper bound yet. Preserving the contour integral does not eliminate them. [Book, Section 5](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:592)

3. **The newest note reaches the scale where local multiplicity matters.**  
   Note 19 retains the entire local zero cluster, including multiplicities, together with the quadratic curvature of the exterior factor. It obtains a complete comparison at offsets of order \(1/\log Y\), even for clusters containing \(O(\log Y)\) zeros. Retaining that curvature fixes a demonstrated order-one error in the simpler approximation.

   Its limitation is important: the small error is measured against the **integral of absolute values**, not the magnitude of the possibly cancelling model integral. Consequently it supplies neither nonvanishing nor a zero-count restriction near a possible multiple zero. [Note 19](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/notes/19_NEAR_AXIS_CLUSTER_AND_QUADRATIC_EXTERIOR_20261023.md:13)

4. **The control example identifies what the missing arithmetic must accomplish.**  
   The book constructs a positive-source field with the same leading zero-count terms and all the coarse estimates used above, yet **every zero has even multiplicity**. It also passes the new near-axis comparison. Thus those estimates cannot alone imply even a positive simple-zero proportion. A successful next estimate must use actual theta arithmetic in a way that changes the bound for this control—not merely name an identity the control lacks. [Book, Proposition 4.1](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:494)

The supporting notes also make useful progress: Hermite domination strengthens the finite-time multiplicity conversion; the Euler-region anchor permits a much larger backward-time interval than the earlier absolute-error argument; and the mollifier calculations rule out leading gains for several precisely specified candidate classes. Those negative results narrow the search without ruling out other arithmetic approaches.

The next substantive advance should therefore be either **a useful bound on the complete resource \(\mathcal R_Y\)** or **an arithmetic restriction on the actual near-axis cluster**. The latter must also control cancellation in its comparison model. Growing-height uniformity, end contributions and coverage remain necessary. Density-one simplicity would still allow sparse multiple zeros; every-zero simplicity requires stronger control.

**Yes—the current book proves an actual moving boundary, depending on both time and spatial position.** I should have made that clearer. “Fixed offset” describes its starting distance from the real axis; its subsequent position moves.

Writing \(z=x+iy\), the upper boundary has the form
\[
\Gamma_t=\{x+i\varepsilon(t,x)\}.
\]
The field determines its motion through
\[
\frac{dZ}{dt}=U(t,Z),
\qquad U(t,z)=\frac{H_z(t,z)}{H(t,z)}.
\]
Boundary points can move horizontally and vertically. Consequently, the graph satisfies
\[
\boxed{\varepsilon_t+\Re(U)\,\varepsilon_x=\Im(U),}
\]
with \(U\) evaluated on the boundary. This allows its shape to vary along its length.

[Book Theorem 3.1](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:366) proves that, under RH, this evolution:

- Exists uniquely for backward times of length \(c/(\log Y)^2\).
- Remains a graph, stays within a controlled spatial region, and covers the target height band.
- Has displacement and slope \(O(1/\log Y)\).
- Moves upward as time runs backward; the reflected lower boundary moves downward.
- Preserves \(H\,dz\) along material arcs and preserves their primitive image.

The boundary is specified by this evolution equation and a proved approximation; there is no elementary closed formula for its shape.

**It is then incorporated directly into the zero-counting argument.** The book uses the moving window
\[
\psi_Y(t,x+iy)
=\eta(x)\,\chi\!\left(\frac{y}{\varepsilon(t,x)}\right).
\]
Its upper and lower transitions follow the moving graphs. The balance includes the time derivative of this window, so boundary motion is explicitly accounted for. Yes. **In the current book, the moving boundary is a curve in the complex \(z\)-plane.** Heat time \(t\) controls how that curve moves. It bounds the region in which we count zeros; \(H(t,z)\) itself remains defined throughout the complex plane.

The project also discusses a different construction—a boundary that assigns a heat time to each height. My previous explanation should have distinguished those more explicitly.

Write \(z=x+iy\). The book uses
\[
H(0,z)=\frac18\xi\!\left(\frac12+\frac{iz}{2}\right).
\]
Consequently, the usual zeta coordinate is
\[
w=\frac{1-y}{2}+i\frac{x}{2}.
\]

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(x=\Re z\) | Twice the usual zeta height |
| \(y=\Im z\) | Displacement across the critical line; \(y=0\) corresponds to that line |
| \(t\) | An independent heat-deformation parameter |

Thus **the critical line appears as the horizontal real axis in our \(z\)-plane**. This rotation of the usual picture is an easy source of confusion.

The upper and lower boundaries have the form
\[
\Gamma_t^\pm=\{x\pm i\varepsilon(t,x)\}.
\]
At each fixed \(t\), these are two spatial curves surrounding part of the real axis. As \(t\) varies, they sweep out surfaces in the three real coordinates \((t,x,y)\). So your idea of a boundary depending on time and spatial position is incorporated: we describe that surface through its spatial cross-sections.

**The motion is chosen to preserve a quantity supplied by the heat equation.** A point \(Z(t)\) on the material boundary follows
\[
\frac{dZ}{dt}=U(t,Z),\qquad U=\frac{H_z}{H}.
\]
It can move horizontally as well as vertically. The resulting curve can nevertheless be represented as a graph \(y=\varepsilon(t,x)\).

To understand what this accomplishes, introduce the primitive
\[
P(t,z)=\int_0^z H(t,w)\,dw.
\]
Along the chosen motion,
\[
\frac{d}{dt}P(t,Z(t))=0.
\]
Each boundary point follows a constant primitive value. Equivalently, the integral of \(H\,dz\) along a transported subarc is preserved.

The book proves that this motion actually exists, stays regular, and continues to cover the desired height interval. Under RH, starting a fixed positive distance from the axis, the upper wall moves upward and the lower wall downward when followed backward over the stated short heat interval. This is the content of the [material-graph theorem](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:366).

But the preserved quantity is a **complex field integral**. A simple zero has its own velocity,
\[
v=\frac{H_{zz}}{H_z},
\]
which generally differs from \(U\). The boundary therefore supplies a controlled moving frame for observation; its conservation law does not force zeros to travel with it.

**The function \(\psi\) turns this geometry into a counting device.** Think of it as a smooth viewing window:
\[
\psi(t,x+iy)
=\eta(x)\,
\chi\!\left(\frac{y}{\varepsilon(t,x)}\right).
\]

Here \(\eta\) selects the height interval, while \(\chi\) follows the upper and lower walls. The weights mean:

- **\(\psi=1\):** count a zero fully.
- **\(0<\psi<1\):** count it fractionally in a transition buffer.
- **\(\psi=0\):** omit it from this localized count.

The geometric wall lies **within** the transition buffer. The buffer softens the sharp distinction between inside and outside, allowing us to differentiate the count as the window and the zeros move. This smoothing changes the observable; it does not alter \(H\) or its zeros.

For example, the weighted nonreal population is
\[
N_{\psi,\mathrm{nr}}(t)
=\sum_{\substack{H(t,z)=0\\ \Im z\ne0}}
m_z\,\psi(t,z).
\]
The restriction “nonreal” is separate from \(\psi\): the window equals one on the real axis throughout the target interval.

For a moving simple zero \(z(t)\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t,z(t))
=
\underbrace{\psi_t}_{\text{window changes}}
+
\underbrace{\nabla\psi\cdot v}_{\text{zero moves}}.
\]
Both terms matter. A stationary point can acquire a larger weight because the window expands around it. Conversely, a moving zero can retain the same weight if its motion matches the window.

This leads to an exact accounting identity:
\[
\text{final nonreal count}+\text{real-collision loss}
=
\text{initial nonreal count}
+\text{inward flux}-\text{outward flux}.
\]
The collision term records nonreal zeros reaching the real axis; those events would be missed by accounting only for crossings of the outer walls.

**The concrete gain is that the book places the upper and lower transition buffers in proved zero-free regions.** There are no zeros where those parts of \(\psi\) change, so they contribute no flux. The remaining terms concern the earlier nonreal population inside the window and crossings near the two height ends. The book explicitly retains both. A fixed wall inside the same zero-free corridor would also eliminate these particular transition contributions; the material construction additionally supplies the conserved evolution. See the [window construction and its limitation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:746).

A simple example explains why the interior population remains essential:
\[
H(t,z)=(z-a)^2-2t.
\]
At negative time, its zeros are \(a\pm i\sqrt{-2t}\). They meet at \(a\) at \(t=0\), forming a double zero. A sufficiently wide window counts both throughout their approach. **They never cross its outer boundary.** The earlier count of two already pays for the collision.

Finally, if you were picturing
\[
t=h(x),
\]
that is a different boundary: it chooses a different heat time at each height. Evaluating \(H(h(\Re z),z)\) generally destroys holomorphicity in \(z\) and introduces additional correction terms. The manuscripts discuss that construction explicitly, but it is not the spatial material boundary proved in the current book. A simple real zero at \(t=0\) stays real for a sufficiently short backward continuation. A multiple real zero behaves differently: it forces nonreal branches immediately before \(t=0\). The book’s local heat analysis gives:

| Multiplicity at the real endpoint | Nonreal branches immediately before it |
|---|---:|
| Simple | 0 |
| Double | 2 |
| Triple | 2 |
| Fourfold | 4 |
| Order \(m\) | \(2\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) |

Thus **endpoint multiplicity leaves a compulsory signature in the earlier nonreal population**. That is why counting changes between real and nonreal zeros can constrain multiplicity. [Book’s local heat lemma.](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:688)

The exact balance separates two quantities:
\[
\underbrace{N_{\mathrm{nr}}(0)}_{\text{nonreal zeros remaining}}
+
\underbrace{B}_{\text{real-collision charges}}
=
N_{\mathrm{nr}}(-S)+F^+-F^-.
\]
Here the counts are weighted by \(\psi\), and \(B\) includes collisions at the endpoint.

The two research objectives ask different questions about this identity:

- **For RH:** prove that no nonreal zeros remain at \(t=0\), with complete coverage. RH permits a pair to collide into a double real zero exactly at \(t=0\).
- **For RH \(\Rightarrow\) simplicity:** endpoint reality is already assumed. We must exclude collisions occurring **exactly at \(t=0\)**.

The book turns this into an explicit multiplicity estimate. If
\[
R=N_{\mathrm{nr}}(-S)+F_{\mathrm{ends}}^+,
\]
and \(M\) is the total multiplicity at nonsimple endpoint zeros in the target band, then
\[
M\le \frac32R.
\]
Moreover, \(R<2\) excludes every multiple endpoint zero in that band. These are already proved consequences of the balance. [Sharp endpoint bounds.](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/manuscript/book.tex:663)

There is an important limitation that supports part of your intuition: **this accounting does not perfectly identify endpoint multiplicity.** Nonreal zeros might collide at an earlier negative time and then separate into simple real zeros before \(t=0\). Such a history also contributes to the resource \(R\). Consequently, a positive or large \(R\) does not establish an endpoint multiple zero; a sufficiently small upper bound can exclude one.

Also, the current theta-specific theorem constructing the zero-free corridor and moving boundary **assumes RH**. We cannot use that theorem as an independent premise to prove RH. The general balance itself does not require RH and could support an RH investigation, but that application would need independently justified geometry and estimates forcing the terminal nonreal population to vanish.

So I would retain its relevance to RH \(\Rightarrow\) simplicity. The unresolved issue is obtaining a strong enough estimate on the **earlier nonreal population plus inward flux**. The multiplicity conversion is already present; the current boundary estimates do not yet supply the required quantitative bound.

Here is the resulting field construction.

For the manuscript’s heat equation \(H_t=-H_{zz}\), with \(z=x+iy\), fix \(\epsilon>0\) and define an initially unnormalized amplitude
\[
\boxed{
A_\epsilon(t,z)=
\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{\pi}}
\frac{H_z(t,z)}{|H(t,z)|^2+\epsilon^2}.
}
\]

Its squared modulus is exactly the regularized zero density already present in the manuscript:
\[
|A_\epsilon|^2=
\frac{\epsilon^2|H_z|^2}
{\pi(|H|^2+\epsilon^2)^2}.
\]

**This field is smooth at the actual zeros.** At a simple zero it is nonzero; at a multiple zero it vanishes at the center, while the surrounding density retains the multiplicity. As \(\epsilon\to0\), the density converges locally to
\[
\sum_a m_a\delta_a.
\]
Thus your intuition that the field need not be singular at zeros works.

The phase supplies the motion. Write \(A_\epsilon=|A_\epsilon|e^{i\theta}\) wherever it is nonzero. Because its denominator is positive,
\[
\theta=\arg H_z.
\]
A simple zero satisfies
\[
\dot a=\frac{H_{zz}}{H_z},
\]
and consequently
\[
\boxed{\dot x=\theta_y,\qquad \dot y=\theta_x.}
\]

So **zero velocity comes from the phase gradient, with the two coordinate derivatives exchanged**. The density gradient alone would not determine that motion. At collisions the individual velocities can diverge, while the field and its current remain smooth.

There is also an exact evolution equation. Set
\[
V_\epsilon=-2\partial_x\partial_y
\log\!\left(|H|^2+\epsilon^2\right).
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
i\partial_t A_\epsilon
=-\partial_x\partial_y A_\epsilon+V_\epsilon A_\epsilon,
\qquad
\Delta V_\epsilon
=-8\pi\partial_x\partial_y|A_\epsilon|^2.
}
\]

These identities follow directly from the heat equation; I checked their algebra symbolically. After rotating coordinates and rescaling time and amplitude, they match the **focusing Davey–Stewartson II equations**. This gives the quantum-field analogy a precise mathematical connection, although it does not establish a new physical interpretation or a novelty claim. [Checked equation convention](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.08814v1). :codex-file-citation{path="/Users/Shared/szp-archive/height-dependent-heat-contours/references/1712.08814v1.pdf" purpose="source"}

Two qualifications matter. The mixed kinetic operator has both positive and negative directions, so a positive-energy argument is still needed. Also, evolving the larger field system requires the appropriate potential boundary data and constraints identifying the actual theta solution.

Your normalization concern remains valid. An equal-weight distribution over infinitely many zeros cannot be a probability measure—even if their average density were constant. A useful formulation is a normalized state in a finite observation region:
\[
\psi_\epsilon=\frac{hA_\epsilon}{\sqrt{Z_\epsilon}},
\qquad
Z_\epsilon=\int h^2|A_\epsilon|^2\,dA.
\]
Here \(h\) is a fixed smooth window. Then \(\int|\psi_\epsilon|^2=1\), and its phase retains the velocity information. Keep \(Z_\epsilon\) alongside \(\psi_\epsilon\) to retain absolute counting mass.

**A moving boundary is unnecessary for this formulation.** A fixed window works, with flux and normalization corrections in its evolution. Those corrections cannot be dropped.

The strongest contribution from *Continuum_sigma* is an observable that actually distinguishes multiplicity. For a finite collection of zeros, let
\[
\nu=\sum_a m_a\delta_a,\qquad N=\sum_a m_a,
\]
and smooth it with the two-dimensional heat kernel: \(\rho_s=K_s*\nu\). Then
